executive_summary: NZD/CAD is at 0.80013, meaning 1 NZD buys 0.80013 CAD, on the gated-store close of 2026-10-02. That is one session after the 2026-10-01 valuation date, and every level in this report is measured from it. The pair is down 1.37% over one month, 0.77% over three months, 1.18% over six months and 0.41% over one year. It sits at the 33rd percentile of its 52-week closing range (0.78606–0.82902) and below its 50-day, 100-day, 200-day and 200-week averages. The main bilateral story is a policy divergence between two central banks that decide on the same days, 2026-10-28 and 2026-12-09. The RBNZ is about 75–80% priced to hike the OCR to 3.00%. The Bank of Canada is priced between 26% and 41% to hike from 2.25%, even though its own trim-median core is 1.95%, below target. Against that, crude near USD 100 moves income from New Zealand, which imports energy and runs a −3.26%-of-GDP current account, to Canada, which exports energy and runs a +1.03% surplus. Both standalone dossiers are bearish against the US dollar: NZD at −0.159 tactically and CAD at −0.2576. The cross is therefore a call on which currency is less weak, and the gap between the two is widest on the strategic horizon (NZD −0.066 against CAD −0.3646). The settled verdict is Bullish tactically (conviction 2, score +0.1285) and Bullish strategically (conviction 3, score +0.2638). We implement it with a long near 0.7990–0.8015, a stop on a daily close below 0.7905, a tactical base target of 0.8110 into the end of October and a strategic base target of 0.8240 by end-Q1 2027. The main caveat comes from the price data and we publish it plainly. The chart is a sequence of lower highs and lower lows from the 0.82962 August high. On 2026-09-02 the RBNZ hiked while the Bank of Canada held, which is the exact joint outcome the tactical thesis needs, and the cross still fell 1.06% that day. That is direct evidence that the policy channel has not reached spot so far.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Valuation gives no cushion to a long and argues mildly against one. On the base dossier's World Bank PPP calculation, NZD/CAD fair value is 0.7921, so the payload spot of 0.80013 is 1.0% rich for the kiwi. That makes this one of the few kiwi crosses where the NZD is not cheap; it is 16.9% cheap against the USD and 15.0% cheap against the AUD. The quote dossier's REER-relative proxy puts NZD/CAD near 0.7496, which leaves spot 6.7% rich. The BIS real effective exchange rates point the same way: NZD at 102.84 (44th percentile of its cached history, flat on the year) against CAD at 96.29 (down 1.67 points on the year and the second-cheapest in the eleven-currency set). The pair already prices a large Canadian discount. The bullish case therefore rests on that discount widening through policy and trade channels, not on mean reversion. Neither leg is stretched enough for valuation to be actionable on either horizon.

market_context.recent_regime: Since August the cross has traded crude, credit and the higher-beta leg, not the rate differential. The RBNZ hiked in July and September and the differential widened from +25bp to +50bp, yet NZD/CAD fell from 0.829 to 0.800. Two sessions show this clearly. On 2026-09-02 the RBNZ hiked while the Bank of Canada held, and the pair fell 87 pips (−1.06%). The kiwi fell that day because Governor Breman said the timing of any further increase was highly uncertain, and October hike odds dropped to about 36% from 65%. On 2026-09-22, Breman's oil warning lifted the pair 37 pips, and the gain was erased in full the next session. The dominant narrative is a New Zealand that imports energy and pays for $100 oil, set against a Canada whose oil windfall is reduced by a USD 11.05 Brent–WTI spread and a USD 14.80 WCS discount, and whose trade is taxed by Section 338 import bans that took effect 2026-09-29.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The policy differential is +50bp in the kiwi's favour: OCR 2.75% (as of 2026-09-25) against the BoC overnight target of 2.25% (as of 2026-09-28). What a rolled long actually earns is the futures-implied premium of 75.2bp a year (CME 6C/6N calendar spread, 6CZ6→6CH7, observed 2026-09-30, 75.7/166.6-day tenors), which combines the rate differential and the cross-currency basis; the 25bp gap to the policy differential is the combined basis and term effect. Carry-to-vol on the estimated 3-month IV of 7.157% is 0.070 on the policy gap and 0.105 on the roll (0.081 and 0.121 on 60-day realised vol of 6.19%); because the IV estimate runs low, the ratios on implied vol are an upper bound. Carry has not been working: over the past month the cross fell 1.37% while a long earned about 0.06% in roll, and over the year −0.41% in price plus roughly 0.5–0.75% in carry leaves total return close to zero. The trade is a divergence trade that carry happens to pay for, and it survives dollar shocks because both legs are dollar-bloc. It is not a carry trade; carry is a cushion and not a reason for the trade.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Adjusted from 0.24 on both horizons (+0.02). Both central banks decide on the same two dates inside the horizon, 2026-10-28 and 2026-12-09, from near-identical policy levels but in opposite directions. The bilateral thesis resolves through this factor and the simultaneity concentrates the repricing.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The gated rates block puts the OCR at 2.75% against the Bank of Canada overnight target at 2.25%, a bilateral policy differential of +50bp in the kiwi's favour, with the 10-year differential at +103.5bp on the matched monthly vintage (NZ 4.71%, Canada 3.675%, both 2026-08-01) and roughly +116bp on the live prints carried in the two dossiers (NZ 5.12%, Canada 3.96%). The trajectory is the point rather than the level: the RBNZ has hiked twice since July and is about 75% priced to go to 3.00% on 2026-10-28, while the Bank of Canada has held for seven consecutive meetings and is priced between 26% and 41% to hike on the same day depending on the venue (CORRA OIS implies a 74% hold and only +7bp of move as of 2026-10-02; a prediction-market board priced 39.1% for 25bp on 2026-09-26; a third screen showed 40.8%). So the market already prices a net widening of the differential on 28 October of roughly 7 to 12bp. Our expectation is the full 25bp, because the RBNZ governor has validated October pricing while the Bank of Canada's own operational core, the trim-median average at 1.95%, sits below target and August employment fell 41,700. The front ends do not price relative convergence at all: the NZ 2-year at 3.92% is 55bp above the Canadian 2-year at 3.37%, within 5bp of the policy gap, with NZ carrying 117bp of hikes above its own policy rate and Canada 112bp above its own. The transmission is direct: a cross with a positive and widening carry differential, where the futures-implied roll pays a long position about 75bp annualised, reprices on delivery rather than on anticipation.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the bilateral rate path is the strongest single argument for the pair. On our path the OCR reaches 3.00% on 2026-10-28 and 3.25% by the first quarter of 2027, while the Bank of Canada delivers 25bp at most and plausibly nothing, which takes the differential from +50bp to between +75bp and +100bp. Both front ends currently embed almost identical tightening premium above their own policy rates - 117bp in New Zealand, 112bp in Canada - so the bilateral question is purely one of relative delivery, and the two banks have opposite reaction-function problems. The RBNZ is hiking against a headline CPI of 4.1% with a sectoral-factor core at 2.7%, near the top of its band; the Bank of Canada is being priced to roughly 3.45% by September 2027 against a trim-median core of 1.95%, below target, with unemployment at 6.4% and a tariff shock that its own governor says cuts fourth-quarter growth below 1%. The dated anchor for the strategic view is 2026-12-09, when the RBNZ publishes a new OCR track at a Monetary Policy Statement - likely lifting the 3.28% peak - while the Bank of Canada issues a bare statement with no projection round. That asymmetry of communication vehicles matters: one bank gets a scheduled opportunity to raise its own published path, the other does not. The risk to the view is that the Canadian two-year already prices the hikes we think will not come, so the convergence trade is partly a wait for a repricing rather than a fresh impulse, and a genuine Canadian core breakout would validate the curve instead.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential runs clearly in the kiwi's favour and the growth differential is mixed, which nets to a modest Bullish. New Zealand's headline CPI is 4.1% year on year with the RBNZ sectoral-factor core at 2.7%; Canada's headline is 3.0% with the Bank of Canada's operational core, the trim-median average, at 1.95% and below target. That is a 75bp core gap, and core is what each central bank actually reacts to, so the gap maps directly onto the policy divergence in Factor 1. Two prints land two days apart inside the tactical window and both point the same way: Canadian September CPI on 2026-10-19, where the gasoline base effect that produced the 3.0% headline is decaying from 22.8% year on year and ex-gasoline inflation is already 2.4%, and New Zealand's September-quarter CPI on 2026-10-21, where consensus is 3.9% but a September rise in Brent of about 5% skews the risk higher. On growth the picture is genuinely split: New Zealand grew 2.55% year on year against Canada's 1.13%, the second weakest in the G10 set, but on the quarter Canada grew 0.82% against New Zealand's 0.25%. Labour markets both disappoint, with New Zealand unemployment at a nine-year high of 5.6% and Canada at 6.4% after shedding 41,700 jobs in August with permanent-employee wage growth halving to 2.0%. The transmission to the pair is through the relative policy reaction rather than through activity: the economy with the higher core inflation is the one whose central bank keeps moving.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months both inflation rates decay as the 2026 fuel spike rolls out of the annual comparison, but they decay toward different floors: New Zealand's core at 2.7% is near the top of the RBNZ band, Canada's at 1.95% is below the midpoint of its target. That means the terminal inflation differential is structural rather than cyclical, and it keeps the relative policy pressure pointing the same way through the horizon. The growth differential also widens in the kiwi's favour, and for a reason that is specific and dated rather than extrapolated: the Bank of Canada governor has put fourth-quarter Canadian growth below 1% if tariffs persist, and the tariffs did not merely persist but escalated to outright import bans on 2026-09-29, against roughly C$20bn of Canadian retaliation from 2026-09-08. New Zealand's drag is a real income shock - gross national disposable income fell 0.4% in the June quarter on a 9.0% terms-of-trade loss - but it is a price effect that reverses if crude converges toward the consensus path, whereas the Canadian drag is a policy regime with no terminal date. The offsets are real: New Zealand unemployment at 5.6% is heading the wrong way, housing is flat to falling, and the RBNZ itself expects inflation back in the band by mid-2027, which caps how long the hiking cycle runs. Confidence is therefore held near the middle of the range.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Adjusted from 0.10/0.05 (−0.02 tactical, −0.01 strategic). Both legs are dollar-bloc commodity currencies with substantial shared global beta, so a large part of the risk impulse cancels inside the cross; what survives is only the beta differential, which is real but smaller than the standalone weights assume.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The kiwi is the higher-beta leg of this cross by a wide margin and the risk complex is deteriorating at the margin, which is a drag on the pair. The Canadian dossier states the structural pattern directly: in risk-off episodes the Canadian dollar weakens against the US dollar but strengthens against the higher-beta Australian, New Zealand and Norwegian dollars, because its US economic linkage anchors it and its equity correlation of roughly -0.2 to -0.3 is the weakest in the commodity bloc. The New Zealand dossier puts the kiwi's observed beta at about 1.8 times the Australian dollar against the US dollar over the latest month, which places it at the opposite end of the same bloc. The marginal deterioration is in credit rather than equities: US high-yield option-adjusted spreads widened 42bp in a month to 302bp while investment grade was static at 83bp, and VIX rose 1.64 points to 16.07 - a rates-led tightening rather than a growth scare, which is exactly the regime in which thin, high-beta currencies underperform without any equity drawdown. Working the other way, the Canadian equity complex is itself soft, with the TSX down 2.85% on the month on banking and mining losses even as energy producers rose, so the Canadian leg is not a haven in any absolute sense. Net, the beta differential dominates and the cross leans lower in a deteriorating-credit tape.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the risk tails are two-sided for this cross and, unusually, they are correlated with the oil tail in a way that partly cancels the beta argument. The bear case for the pair is a rates-led credit tightening in which the higher-beta kiwi underperforms the US-anchored loonie, consistent with the historical pattern. The bull case is that the dominant risk driver in this cycle is an energy supply shock rather than a demand shock, and a resolution of it - which would be unambiguously risk-positive - is simultaneously the largest terms-of-trade negative for Canada and the largest positive for New Zealand. In other words, the risk-off scenario that hurts the kiwi more also tends to arrive with higher crude, which helps the loonie twice, while the risk-on scenario that helps the kiwi more tends to arrive with lower crude, which hurts the loonie twice. Those two channels are of similar size and they run in the same direction as each other, which means Factor 3 and Factor 5 are not independent and treating both as directional would double-count. With China's manufacturing PMI back at 50.1 and credit still benign at 302bp in absolute terms, there is no signal strong enough to carry either tail. The honest strategic stance is Neutral and the directional content is left in Factor 5 where it belongs.

On the kiwi side, speculative positioning flipped from net long to net short in the week to 2026-09-22, with asset managers swinging 21,655 contracts to a net short of 11,485 and leveraged funds adding 3,021 to a net short of 4,787 - slow money selling into a falling market, with the 25-delta risk reversal moving from about -0.34 to -0.85 vols over the month. Fresh kiwi selling against persistent loonie covering is a two-sided drag on NZD/CAD over four weeks. The level data complicate the story and are the reason confidence stays low: at -11.4K all-spec the kiwi short is only 56% through a two-month range whose extreme was -39.6K, so it has room to extend; at -46,861 the Canadian leveraged short is still large in absolute notional, about USD 3.3bn, and the Canadian dossier notes the covering produced no appreciation at all, which it reads as a bearish tell for the loonie rather than a bullish one. Net, the tactical flow signal is negative for the pair but shallow.

tactical.what_is_priced: Positioning prices a modest short in both legs, which largely cancels in the cross. What is not cancelled is the direction of travel - fresh kiwi selling against loonie covering - and that is a four-week drag rather than a level signal.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two positions are both inside their own normal ranges and neither offers an extreme to revert from, so the combined signal is noise. The kiwi all-spec net of -11.4K sits roughly 28K contracts short of the August extreme near -39.6K, so it can extend; the Canadian leveraged net of -46,861 is 27,000 contracts inside the -80K level the Canadian brief treats as significant and has roughly 42,000 contracts of room to rebuild toward its own August extreme. Both can get more short, which means both can squeeze, and in a cross the two squeezes would partly offset. The structural flows are small and roughly balanced: New Zealand dairy export receipts are a steady commercial kiwi bid with merchandise exports up 15.4% year on year in August, while Canadian portfolio repatriation and Q4 producer energy hedging are a steady loonie bid, the latter weakened this year because hedge ratios rise against a high strip and the crude strip is falling. There is no distinct NZD/CAD community analogous to the yen carry trade, no meaningful ETF in either currency, and the cross is thin enough that futures positioning in the two USD legs is the only observable. With neither leg crowded and the structural flows offsetting, Neutral is the honest answer.

strategic.what_is_priced: Neither futures position carries a squeeze premium, and the six-month kiwi skew of about -0.96 vols already prices a downside tail in the USD leg. There is no crowded trade to fade in either direction on this cross.

factors.horizon_split: Bearish tactically, Neutral strategically. Tactically the signal is the direction of the weekly flow - kiwi shorts being added by slow money while loonie shorts are covered - which is observable and current. Strategically the level is what matters, and both legs sit mid-range inside their own thresholds with symmetric room to extend, so the combined cross signal collapses to nothing.

tactical.combined_positioning_signal: Both legs net short in the futures, so the pair-level net is close to flat: a kiwi all-spec short of 11,380 contracts against a Canadian leveraged short of 46,861 in a market with three times the open interest. The directional information is in the flow, not the stock - fresh kiwi selling against loonie covering - which is a mild drag on the cross rather than a crowded trade in it.
tactical.unwind_trigger: A hot New Zealand Q3 CPI on 2026-10-21 at or above 4.1% followed by an RBNZ hike on 2026-10-28, landing on the same day as a Bank of Canada hold with a lowered oil assumption. That combination forces the 21,655-contract asset-manager swing in the kiwi to reverse while removing the Canadian hike premium, and it is the one dated sequence that squeezes both legs in the same direction for the pair.
tactical.historical_analogue: The August 2026 kiwi cover, when the all-spec net moved roughly 50K contracts from -39.6K to +10.5K in about four weeks and NZD/USD rose roughly two big figures. The Canadian analogue cuts the other way and is the more instructive one: 42,036 contracts of loonie shorts were bought back between 2026-08-18 and 2026-09-22 and produced no Canadian dollar appreciation at all, which says the marginal buyer of CAD is a stopped-out short rather than a fresh long.
tactical.contrarian_case: The crowd is short both currencies against the dollar, which means the consensus is a dollar view rather than a cross view, and nobody is positioned for the cross itself. The contrarian trade is therefore not to fade either short but to note that the one genuinely crowded idea - that the Bank of Canada is about to begin a hiking cycle, priced to roughly 3.45% by September 2027 - rests on a core measure of 1.95% that is below target, and a repricing of that is a pure NZD/CAD event with no dollar component.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: Neutral and genuinely so. Both legs sit inside their own significance thresholds with roughly symmetric room to extend - 28K contracts for the kiwi, 42K for the loonie - so any squeeze in one is plausibly matched by an extension in the other and the cross nets out.
strategic.unwind_trigger: A full capitulation of the published Canadian dollar consensus. Six of seven banks surveyed on 2026-09-28 forecast USD/CAD below spot for Q4 2026, averaging 1.40, which embeds a constructive loonie view; forecast revisions run on quarterly publication cycles rather than margin calls, so the unwind would be a grind rather than a spike, and it would lift NZD/CAD without any kiwi flow at all.
strategic.historical_analogue: The March 2018 episode, when a NAFTA-driven repricing of Canadian trade risk and a convergence of Canadian core inflation on target drove bank forecasts for NZD/CAD toward 0.89 on an explicitly bilateral thesis. The direction of the trade-policy shock has since inverted, and the same channel now runs the other way.
strategic.contrarian_case: The strategic consensus on both legs is that each currency is cheap against the dollar and will recover, which is a statement about the dollar and not about this cross. For NZD/CAD the only positions that matter are the implicit ones in the rates markets: roughly 120bp of Bank of Canada tightening priced against a sub-target core, and an RBNZ track the market already runs 45 percentage points ahead of. Both are vulnerable, but only the Canadian one is vulnerable in the direction nobody is hedged for.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Adjusted from 0.06/0.16 (+0.03 on both horizons). This is a commodity-exporter versus commodity-exporter cross in which the dominant commodity cuts in exactly opposite directions - New Zealand is a net energy importer and Canada is a net energy exporter - so crude is a pure bilateral variable here rather than a shared one, and it is the single largest non-policy driver of the pair.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Crude at roughly USD 100 Brent is a direct income transfer from the base economy to the quote economy and it is the clearest bilateral fact on this pair. New Zealand's terms of trade fell 9.0% in the June quarter against an expected 2.2% fall, because import prices rose 13.8% while export prices rose 3.5%, and real gross national disposable income fell 0.4% as a result; Canada posted its first current account surplus since 2022 at C$8.8bn on record energy exports of C$60.6bn, with crude and bitumen at a record C$44.8bn. On levels, Canada runs +1.03% of GDP against New Zealand's -3.26%, a 4.3-point gap. Two things blunt the transfer and are the reason this is a 55 and not a 65. First, Canada realises a landlocked barrel: the Brent-WTI spread was USD 11.05 on 2026-09-30, nearly triple the USD 4.08 of a year earlier, and Western Canadian Select settles USD 14.80 under WTI, so the realised Canadian barrel is near USD 76.70 against a USD 100-plus global headline. Second, New Zealand's own export complex is firm, with Fonterra lifting its 2026/27 farmgate midpoint to NZ$9.50/kgMS and the August trade deficit coming in at NZ$1.35bn against a NZ$1.78bn estimate on exports up 15.4%. Bilateral trade itself is immaterial: New Zealand exported USD 0.7bn of goods to Canada in 2024 against USD 0.4bn imported, a net USD 0.2bn balance, which is a rounding error in either current account and creates no structural flow. Two GDT auctions on 2026-10-06 and 2026-10-20 and the Canadian August trade print on 2026-10-06 are the dated tests.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices crude near USD 100 and dairy at current levels, which is the configuration that favours the quote currency. The two October GDT auctions and the Canadian August trade print are two-sided events on which we have no directional edge.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the external factor is finely balanced and that is the honest reading rather than an evasion, even at a 0.19 weight. The levels favour Canada decisively - a surplus against a deficit projected to widen toward 4.5% of GDP - but every element of the Canadian surplus is a price effect in a price that the consensus path has falling: the Reuters September poll puts 2026 averages at USD 89.05 Brent and USD 83.90 WTI, both below the latest prints, and the Canadian dossier itself expects the quarterly surplus to shrink toward C$2-5bn. On the kiwi side the same path reverses the income transfer, and dairy, which is about a quarter of New Zealand goods exports, is firm enough for Fonterra to have raised rather than cut its forecast. Two structural constraints bind the Canadian side and do not bind the New Zealand side: a pipeline-takeaway tax, visible as the USD 14.80 WCS discount, which caps revenue capture regardless of the Brent level, and a tariff regime that taxes the very goods balance that produced the surplus, with 66.3% of Canadian goods exports going to a single counterparty. Valuation leans the same way without being actionable: the kiwi's BIS real effective exchange rate is 102.84 at the 44th percentile of its cached history, against Canada at 96.29 and at the bottom of the commodity bloc, so neither is expensive and the Canadian discount is the deeper one. With the level favouring Canada and the trajectory favouring New Zealand, the factor abstains.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices a persistent energy premium that Canada monetises and New Zealand pays for. We think only half of that is true - Canada monetises a discounted barrel - but we have no edge on the crude path itself, and the crude path is what decides this factor.

factors.horizon_split: Bearish tactically, Neutral strategically. Tactically the transfer is happening now at a Brent price above USD 100 and a realised Canadian surplus already printed, so the factor pushes the cross lower. Strategically the consensus crude path is below spot, which reverses the transfer, and Canada's capture of any remaining premium is structurally capped by a USD 14.80 WCS discount and a live tariff regime - so the level and the trajectory point opposite ways and cancel.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: New Zealand: dairy is about a quarter of goods exports, with the GDT index at an average winning price of USD 3,868/t at Event 412 and Fonterra's 2026/27 farmgate midpoint raised to NZ$9.50/kgMS; meat and forestry secondary. Crucially New Zealand is a NET ENERGY IMPORTER with no offsetting crude export, so higher oil is a pure cost with no revenue side.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: Canada: crude oil and bitumen at a record C$44.8bn of quarterly exports, total energy exports C$60.6bn, plus natural gas with Henry Hub at USD 2.90, lumber and potash. A NET ENERGY EXPORTER, but one that realises WTI at Hardisty less a USD 14.80 Western Canadian Select discount rather than the waterborne Brent price.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Apply the direction rules leg by leg. Oil up gives ++CAD for the quote currency and a clean negative for the base currency, because New Zealand has the importer exposure of the rule set with none of the mild commodity-currency offset that applies to Australia - New Zealand exports no crude. Both signs therefore push the same way and NZD/CAD FALLS on higher oil, making this one of the few G10 crosses where the dominant commodity is unambiguous and non-cancelling. Dairy up gives ++NZD with no Canadian exposure at all, so NZD/CAD RISES, but the dairy move is secondary in magnitude: Brent is up 56.85% year on year while the GDT index has moved less than 1% at each of the last two auctions. Two second-order adjustments reduce the gross oil sensitivity by perhaps a third. First, Canada captures only the WTI-minus-WCS barrel near USD 76.70, so a given Brent move transmits attenuated. Second, higher oil raises New Zealand tradables inflation - petrol was up 20.1% quarter on quarter and diesel 47.7% - which raises RBNZ hike odds and partly offsets the terms-of-trade loss through Factor 1. Net exposure: the pair is a short-crude, long-dairy expression, with crude dominant.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Brent to about USD 110. New Zealand's current account deficit widens toward 4.5-5% of GDP with another quarter of falling real national income, while Canadian energy export values rise from an already record base. Attenuated by the USD 11.05 Brent-WTI spread and the USD 14.80 WCS discount on the Canadian side and by higher RBNZ hike odds on the New Zealand side, the net effect is roughly 1.5-2.5% lower for NZD/CAD rather than the 3-4% a naive netting would give.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Brent to about USD 90, converging on the consensus path. The New Zealand terms-of-trade loss begins to reverse and the import bill falls, while the Canadian surplus shrinks and - this is the amplifier - the Bank of Canada's own stated precondition for tightening, oil near USD 100, recedes further out of reach, so the commodity channel and the guidance channel fire together. Net effect roughly 2-3% higher for NZD/CAD, meaningfully larger than the symmetric case.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Crude oil, specifically the WTI price and the WCS differential rather than the Brent headline. Dairy via the fortnightly GDT auction is the secondary driver and the only one that moves the base leg in isolation.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks have turned hawkish in communication, but one of them conditioned its hawkishness on a number that has already failed and the other did not. The RBNZ hiked unanimously by consensus on 2026-09-02 and Governor Breman then said that persistent oil prices would produce somewhat higher near-term inflation than the September Statement assumed, which lifted October hike pricing from about 57% to about 75% - the market now runs ahead of the published 3.28% track because the Governor invited it to, and the RBNZ has a strong record of not leaning against pricing it has itself validated. Governor Macklem's Halifax warning on 2026-09-21 against being too slow to respond was explicitly tied to oil staying near USD 100 per barrel, and WTI settled at USD 91.51 on 2026-09-30, 8.5% below that threshold, with the consensus path lower again. The vehicles differ in a way that matters for the pair: on 2026-10-28 the RBNZ publishes a Monetary Policy Review, a decision without a new track, while the Bank of Canada publishes a full Monetary Policy Report with a new inflation model and must therefore print an oil assumption the market can measure against the governor's own threshold. A bank that has to publish a lowered oil assumption against a hawkish conditional commitment is walking guidance back; a bank that only has to deliver a hike it has already endorsed is not. Credibility is high on both sides, which is precisely why the asymmetry bites.

BoC: Macklem conditioned the hiking bias on oil near USD 100 on 2026-09-21; WTI settled USD 91.51 on 2026-09-30, 8.5% below the stated precondition
Governing Council found little evidence of gasoline pass-through to other prices at the 2026-09-02 meeting and made any response conditional on spillover into core, which has not occurred
Vehicle asymmetry on 2026-10-28: RBNZ Monetary Policy Review (decision only) versus BoC Monetary Policy Report (full projection round, debuting a new inflation model)
tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices both governors as committed hawks. Only one of them attached a falsifiable number to the commitment, and that number has already failed four weeks before the meeting at which he must publish a forecast against it.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the communication asymmetry persists and acquires a second dated vehicle. On 2026-12-09 the RBNZ publishes a Monetary Policy Statement with a new OCR track, the first opportunity to lift the 3.28% peak toward the 3.50% that the sell side already carries, while the Bank of Canada issues a bare statement with no projection round and therefore no scheduled mechanism for formally raising its own path before 2027. Transparency levels are comparable - both banks publish forecasts, both publish deliberations or equivalent, both have documented neutral-rate estimates - so this is not a credibility gap but a calendar-and-content gap. The counterweight is real and keeps confidence near the middle: the RBNZ's own language describes a short cycle with inflation back in the band by mid-2027, the New Zealand 2-year at 3.92% already prices more than the bank is likely to deliver, and the 2026-11-07 election adds a fiscal variable to the RBNZ reaction function. On the Canadian side the symmetric risk is that a Hormuz re-escalation restores Macklem's USD 100 precondition and retrospectively vindicates both his guidance and the market's 120bp of pricing, which would flip this factor cleanly. That is a crude-price bet rather than a communication judgement, and it is scored in Factor 5.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices a Bank of Canada that follows through on Halifax and an RBNZ that stops near 3.25%. We think the RBNZ gets a scheduled chance to raise its own track in December and the Bank of Canada does not, which is a structural asymmetry the pricing does not reflect.

factors.horizon_split: Both horizons Bullish, confidence easing from 58 to 54. Tactically the resolution is dated and the vehicle is specific: the Bank of Canada must publish an oil assumption on 2026-10-28 against a threshold its own governor named. Strategically the same asymmetry runs through a December in which only one of the two banks has a projection round, but it has to survive six months and a crude-price tail that would vindicate the Canadian guidance wholesale.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The event risk on this cross is sharply asymmetric and it falls on the quote currency. US Section 338 measures against Canadian imports escalated from a 50% ad valorem duty to outright import bans effective 2026-09-29, two days before the valuation date, covering dairy, alcoholic beverages and motor vehicles, with USMCA providing no relief and the duties stacking on existing antidumping, countervailing and Section 232 measures; Canada retaliated on 2026-09-08 with roughly C$20bn of tariffs. That is a realised shock, not a risk, and its first measurable prints land inside the tactical window on 2026-10-06 for trade and 2026-10-09 for employment. New Zealand's event set is denser but milder and more two-sided: two GDT auctions on 2026-10-06 and 2026-10-20, the Q3 CPI on 2026-10-21, and a general election on 2026-11-07 just beyond the window, where the September poll projected 64 seats for the governing bloc against 56 and a clear result would be close to neutral for the currency. The shared geopolitical variable is the Strait of Hormuz, and it is not shared symmetrically: an escalation is a tax on the New Zealand import bill and a windfall for Canadian producers, while a settlement reverses both. That single variable is the main downside to a Bullish stance here, which is why confidence sits at 56 rather than higher.

Canadian retaliation of approximately C$20bn from 2026-09-08, including 50% on steel and aluminium
New Zealand general election 2026-11-07: September poll projects 64 of 120 seats for the governing bloc against 56, margin of error 3.1 points - a close but not disorderly outcome
Shared and asymmetric: a Hormuz settlement taking Brent below USD 85 is kiwi-positive and loonie-negative; an escalation above USD 115 is the reverse
tactical.what_is_priced: The tariff regime is priced as a level effect already embedded in a cheap Canadian dollar, not as an escalating process - and it escalated two days before the valuation date, with the first hard evidence due on 2026-10-06 and 2026-10-09.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the asymmetry deepens because the Canadian exposure is architectural rather than episodic. The United States declined the sixteen-year USMCA extension at the 2026-07-01 joint review, so the agreement no longer renews automatically and instead runs on annual review cycles through to a 2036 expiry, with US demands including 50% US content in North American vehicles. For an economy sending 66.3% of its goods exports to one counterparty, converting a settled treaty into an annually renegotiated one is a permanent increase in the risk premium on its assets, and it is the most plausible explanation for the Canadian real effective exchange rate falling 1.67 points over twelve months while every other commodity currency was re-rated. New Zealand carries nothing comparable: there is no live trade dispute, it supplies 49% of China's dairy imports by value with exports to China up 15.8% year on year, and its US-bound exports are small enough that tariff risk is peripheral. The New Zealand strategic events are an election resolving in November, possible coalition talks into late November, and a December policy statement - all ordinary. The offsetting catalyst, and the principal risk to this stance, is the USTR's stated end-2026 target for interim USMCA deals: a suspension of the import bans would remove the single largest standing negative on the quote leg in one headline.

strategic.what_is_priced: No published Canadian dollar forecast embeds either a permanent tariff regime or its resolution, so the market prices a middling path on a binary. For the cross, the standing risk premium on Canadian assets is the part that is underpriced.

factors.horizon_split: Both horizons Bullish, confidence rising from 56 to 58 - an unusual direction, and it reflects that the Canadian exposure is architectural rather than episodic. Tactically the import bans are two days old and their first hard evidence is dated. Strategically an annually renegotiated treaty is a standing premium on one leg of the cross and nothing equivalent exists on the other, and the only thing that removes it is a USTR deal the market has not priced in either direction.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Neither sovereign is a driver of this cross over four weeks and the differential, such as it is, is small and offsetting. New Zealand carries Moody's Aaa with S&P and Fitch at AA+, all stable, with net core Crown debt projected to peak at 46.1% of GDP in 2027/28 and an OBEGALx surplus pencilled for 2028/29. Canada carries Moody's Aaa, S&P AAA and DBRS AAA with Fitch at AA+, so it is marginally the better-rated of the two, and its federal debt at roughly 42-43% of GDP is slightly lower than New Zealand's peak - but its general government figure including provinces runs 91.8% of GDP in 2026 against an AA median near 50%. Neither bond market shows a sovereign premium: the New Zealand 10-year at 5.12% trades 12bp below US Treasuries, and the Canadian 10-year at 3.96% sits on a smoothly upward-sloping curve with no auction stress. No rating agency has either sovereign on review. The only dated fiscal item inside the window on either side is New Zealand election campaign spending commitments, which have not moved the bond market, and the monthly Canadian budget balance, which deteriorated to -C$4.77bn but is an order of magnitude too small to matter for a currency pair.

tactical.what_is_priced: Both sovereigns are priced as high-grade with no premium, which is correct. Nothing in either fiscal calendar argues for a change inside four weeks.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months both fiscal trajectories deteriorate and they do so from different directions, which keeps the bilateral signal at zero. Canada's general government debt path from 88.6% of GDP in 2024 to a projected 98.5% in 2027 is the larger absolute deterioration and drew an explicit warning from Fitch that persistent fiscal expansion has weakened the credit profile, though that commentary is now well over a year old and the federal figure near 43% remains low by G10 standards. New Zealand's post-election Half-Year Update in December is the first fiscal forecast after a vote in which a change of government would probably loosen policy, and the Budget's 2028/29 surplus was built on lower yields than the 10-year's 91bp twelve-month rise now implies. Crucially, in both cases a looser fiscal stance is mildly supportive of the respective currency through the rates channel, because each central bank would have to lean against it - so even the directional fiscal risks partly cancel in the cross. The factor would only become material through an actual rating action, which we put at roughly 15% for Canada and lower for New Zealand inside the horizon, or through a housing bust or natural disaster in New Zealand, neither of which is a base case. Neutral at 52 is the defensible reading.

strategic.what_is_priced: Both sovereigns are priced at zero risk premium and we agree. The only unpriced element is a Canadian agency action on a confirmed 98.5% debt path, which would begin to matter at the following review rather than inside this horizon.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral on both horizons, with confidence easing from 55 to 52 because the strategic window contains a New Zealand election, a post-election Half-Year Update and a possible Canadian rating review, none of which has a dated resolution. The structural point holds on both horizons: the two sovereigns are close enough in quality, and their respective risks offsetting enough, that nothing transmits to the cross.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This pass is deliberately not given the chart, so the honest stance on the one factor for which the chart is legitimate evidence is Neutral. What the payload does carry at pair level is a volatility and liquidity picture, and it is unremarkable. Estimated at-the-money implied volatility is 7.331% at 36.7 days and 7.157% at 99.7 days, essentially flat across the two tenors, with no event hump at the front despite a calendar containing two central-bank decisions on the same day. That estimate is a triangle construction from the two USD legs using a realised correlation of 0.5626 standing in for an unobservable implied one, a substitution that has historically run 9-18% low, so the true surface is probably nearer 7.8-8.4% and the flatness is more reliable than the level. The structural fact that matters most is liquidity: NZD/CAD has no listed option anywhere, so there is no quoted surface, no risk reversal and no barrier information, and the cross is traded as two dollar legs by most participants. The gated store also flags a zone shortfall, with only 6 resistance and 2 support clusters meeting the two-touch threshold, which independently says this pair spends less time building order density than a major. Without trend, range-position or level data, there is nothing here that can or should move a stance.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar conditions are the one global factor that does not cancel in this cross, because the two currencies are differently exposed to it. The dollar is strengthening on the exceptionalism side of its smile rather than on funding scarcity: SOFR printed 3.88% on USD 2.967tn of volume with a 16bp percentile dispersion inside a 3.75-4.00% band, reserves stand at USD 2.93tn, balance-sheet runoff ended in December 2025 and the Fed is buying bills, while the broad dollar index rose 1.884 points in a month to 120.33 and the US 10-year rose 51bp to 5.24%. In that regime the relevant bilateral question is which leg is the worse funding credit, and it is the kiwi: New Zealand has no standing swap line with the Federal Reserve, runs a 3.2%-of-GDP current account deficit that must be funded from abroad, and is the smaller and thinner market, while Canada has a standing and unused Fed line and the deepest banking linkage to the United States of any G10 economy. The mechanism is not funding stress - there is none - but the absence of a stress ceiling on a dollar grind that penalises the more externally dependent of the two. Against that, the New Zealand futures-implied basis residual is only about -3bp, so there is no measurable kiwi funding premium today, which caps how negative this factor can honestly be scored.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of +0.1285 on a -1.0 to +1.0 scale is at the lower end of the Bullish band, meaning the pair is expected to rise but without depth behind the call. Four factors are Bullish (Policy and Rates +0.1508, Inflation and Growth +0.0954, Guidance +0.0406, Event Risk +0.0280, together +0.3148) against four Bearish (Flows -0.0520, External Balance -0.0495, Risk Appetite -0.0432, USD Liquidity -0.0416, together -0.1863) and two abstentions. Breadth is not doing the work here - the split is four against four - and depth barely is either: Policy and Rates alone contributes more than the whole net score, so if that factor is wrong the verdict inverts. The four negatives are also not independent of each other: higher crude, a firmer dollar, wider credit spreads and slow money selling the higher-beta leg are substantially one mechanism, which means they could all reverse together on a single crude or Fed headline. That coherence cuts both ways and is the main reason conviction is held at 2.
tactical.rationale: At the applied tactical weights the book is decided by Policy and Rates at 0.26, Inflation and Growth at 0.18, Flows at 0.10 and External Balance at 0.09, and the first two of those are the only factors generating genuine depth. The dominant mechanism is a bilateral policy differential of +50bp that is set to widen on a single session: on 2026-10-28 the RBNZ is roughly 75% priced to hike to 3.00% and the Bank of Canada is priced between 26% and 41% to hike, with CORRA overnight index swaps implying a 74% hold and only +7bp of move as of 2026-10-02, so the market prices roughly 7 to 12bp of net widening against the 25bp we expect. That is the edge, and it is small, specific and dated. It is reinforced by a core inflation gap that runs the same way - 2.7% on the RBNZ sectoral factor model against 1.95% on the Bank of Canada trim-median average, with the Canadian measure below target - and by a guidance asymmetry in which Governor Macklem's hawkish bias was explicitly conditioned on oil near USD 100 while WTI settled at USD 91.51, four weeks before he must publish an oil assumption in a full Monetary Policy Report. The two dossiers reinforce rather than conflict: both currencies are Bearish standalone against the dollar, at -0.159 for the kiwi and -0.2576 for the loonie, so the cross is a relative-weakness call in which the kiwi is the less damaged leg by roughly a tenth of a score point. The bilateral factors that modify the standalone views pull both ways. In the kiwi's favour, the Section 338 import bans that took effect 2026-09-29 and the annual USMCA review cycle are a standing tax on the quote leg with no New Zealand equivalent. Against it, crude near USD 100 is a direct income transfer from a 3.26%-of-GDP deficit economy to a 1.03%-of-GDP surplus economy, speculative flow is selling the kiwi while covering the loonie, and the kiwi is the higher-beta leg into widening high-yield spreads. What is priced is a double central-bank decision with both outcomes partly discounted; what we expect is the modal joint outcome of a kiwi hike and a Canadian hold, which is worth more than the pricing implies because the two probabilities are close to independent. The path of least resistance is a drift higher into the 19-21 October CPI pair and a step at the 28 October double decision. The dated catalysts are 2026-10-06 (GDT Event 413 and Canadian August trade), 2026-10-09 (Canadian labour force survey), 2026-10-19 (Canadian CPI), 2026-10-20 (GDT Event 414), 2026-10-21 (New Zealand Q3 CPI) and 2026-10-28 (both central banks). Conviction is 2 rather than 3 because the four negative factors share a single crude-and-dollar mechanism that could reverse them together, because the estimated vol surface prices no event premium at all for a month this dense, and because a Hormuz escalation would restore the Bank of Canada's own stated hiking precondition and flip Factors 5, 6 and 1 in one move. PASS-2 NOTE ON THE VERDICT (price data, published disagreement; the score stands): The price payload contains a direct test of the tactical mechanism, and the result is uncomfortable. On 2026-09-02 the RBNZ hiked and the Bank of Canada held on the same day, which is the 'modal joint outcome' this rationale relies on, and NZD/CAD fell 87 pips (−1.06%). The reason was guidance, not the decision: the RBNZ published a track pointing to an October pause. The differential has widened by 25bp since July, yet the cross has fallen from 0.82902 to 0.80013. In our judgement the market has been trading this pair on crude and kiwi beta, not on relative policy. The verdict can still be right, because 2026-10-28 is an RBNZ Review with no track while the Bank of Canada has to publish an oil assumption. But the tactical call depends on guidance, not just on delivery. Our practical test is this: if both banks deliver the expected outcome on 2026-10-28 and the pair cannot hold a daily close above 0.8059, the tactical verdict should be treated as wrong regardless of its score.

November should consolidate in 0.8050–0.8150 around the 2026-11-07 election and GDT 415 (2026-11-03), with pullbacks finding support at the 200-day average (0.80996) and the top of the six-touch band (0.8059). Step two is 2026-12-09: if the RBNZ raises its track while the Bank of Canada, without a projection round, fails to deliver a hike that is close to fully priced, the pair should reach the lower edge of the ten-touch band at 0.8170 by year-end. The final leg runs through the January 2027 Canadian MPR and the 2027-03-17 RBNZ MPS, grinding toward 0.8240 and a weekly close back above the rising 200-week. Volatility should stay near 6–7% realised outside event days. Expect one counter-move of 120–180 pips, most likely on a crude spike or a USMCA headline. A weekly close below 0.7840 means the step pattern has failed.

increase_conditions: Increase to 4 if: (a) the RBNZ track peak is raised to 3.50% or more at the 2026-12-09 MPS while the Bank of Canada holds at 2.25% the same day; (b) WTI averages below USD 88 through November with the WCS discount at USD 14 or wider.
Increase to 5 if: (a) the policy differential reaches +100bp; (b) the USMCA review or Section 338 escalates to energy or autos while Brent is below USD 90.
decrease_conditions: Decrease to 2 if: (a) the Bank of Canada hikes on 2026-10-28 or 2026-12-09 and the RBNZ does not hike at the same meeting; (b) WTI closes above USD 100 for five sessions with Brent–WTI inside USD 6; (c) Canadian trim-median rises above 2.4%.

Decrease to 1 if: (a) a USTR–Canada interim deal suspends the import bans and the Bank of Canada hikes; (b) a weekly close below 0.7840, or NZ unemployment at 6.0% or higher in the 2026-11-W1 HLFS combined with an RBNZ pause signal.

consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Bullish, net score +0.1285, conviction 2, overall confidence 55. The pair rises modestly over four weeks (base target 0.8110) as the 28 October double decision delivers a 25bp widening of the policy differential against the 7-12bp priced.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bullish, net score +0.2638, conviction 3, overall confidence 58. The differential widens from +50bp toward +75/+100bp over six months (base target 0.8240 by end-Q1 2027) as the RBNZ delivers and the Bank of Canada underdelivers against roughly 120bp of embedded tightening.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Above the implied consensus on both horizons, and materially so strategically.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Pass 1: not quantifiable in pips, as that pass sets no levels. In policy terms the divergence is 25 to 50bp of relative delivery over six months: the market has the two banks tightening by broadly similar amounts, and we have the RBNZ delivering 50bp while the Bank of Canada delivers 0 to 25bp. Against the indirect bank anchors - a 1.40 average USD/CAD forecast for Q4 2026 implying loonie strength, against a mildly constructive kiwi path - we are on the opposite side of the Canadian leg and the same side of the New Zealand leg. Pass 2 quantification against the published pair numbers: the only pair-level figures available are retail and model outputs, and they disagree with each other. The aggregator page has NZD/CAD at 0.83 for year-end 2026, rising to 0.87 by mid-2027, but that is based on two providers and the page is about eight months old. Model sites point the other way: one model projects 0.7722 by end-2026, and another forecasts −0.87% over one year. Our tactical 0.8110 (+97 pips) and strategic 0.8240 (+227 pips) sit between them: about 340–520 pips above the model sites and about 60 pips below the stale aggregator's 0.83 Q4 figure.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: We weigh two bilateral factors differently from the implied consensus. First, Guidance and Credibility: the consensus reads both governors as equally committed hawks, but only Governor Macklem attached a falsifiable number to his commitment, oil near USD 100, and that precondition has already failed with WTI at USD 91.51 and a consensus path of USD 83.90, while Governor Breman's oil remark pushed market pricing above her own published track and the RBNZ has a record of validating pricing it has endorsed. Second, External Balance: the consensus reads Canada's record C$8.8bn quarterly surplus as a structural re-rating, whereas Canada realises a landlocked barrel near USD 76.70 after an USD 11.05 Brent-WTI spread and an USD 14.80 WCS discount, so the windfall is both smaller than the headline and a function of a price the same consensus forecasts lower. Third and underweighted everywhere: an annually renegotiated USMCA with import bans live from 2026-09-29 is a standing risk premium on the quote leg that no published forecast embeds in either direction. Sell-side OCR paths give the RBNZ leg real support: ANZ expects three hikes (October, February, March) to 3.5%, BNZ sees sequential hikes to 3.75% by March 2027, and Kiwibank and Westpac see just two more, to 3%. The Canadian rates market, by contrast, has moved toward our opposite: late-September pricing for 28 October was close to a coin flip, from roughly 94% hold odds before the September decision.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: A widening of the bilateral policy differential from +50bp to +75/+100bp over six months, delivered through two scheduled decision pairs, on a cross where a long position is additionally paid roughly 75bp annualised by the futures-implied roll. The expression is clean because it strips out the dollar and the risk beta that dominate both legs individually. Pair-level payoff if right: +227 pips plus about 30 pips of carry.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: The specific way this loses is a Hormuz escalation that takes crude back above USD 100 with a narrower Brent-WTI spread. That single event restores the Bank of Canada's stated hiking precondition, validates the roughly 120bp of Canadian tightening in the curve, deepens New Zealand's terms-of-trade loss and widens its current account deficit - flipping Factors 1, 5 and 6 together. A secondary loss case is a USTR-Canada interim deal by end-2026 that suspends the Section 338 import bans and removes the standing premium on the quote leg. If wrong the strategic loss is −161 pips at the strategic stop.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: Aligned in direction and strengthening with time (tactical conviction 2, net score +0.1285; strategic conviction 3, net score +0.2638), which is unusual and worth naming. The same mechanism drives both horizons - relative policy delivery between two banks that decide on the same dates - but three things that cap the call tactically decay over the strategic window. Risk Appetite is Bearish over four weeks on a measured 42bp of high-yield widening and the kiwi's higher beta, but Neutral over six months because the risk tail and the crude tail turn out to be the same tail and carrying both would double-count. Flows is Bearish tactically on the direction of weekly positioning - fresh kiwi selling against loonie covering - but Neutral strategically because both legs sit mid-range with symmetric room to extend. External Balance is Bearish tactically because the income transfer is happening now at crude above USD 100, but Neutral strategically because the consensus crude path is below spot and Canada's capture is structurally capped. Meanwhile the positive side gains weight: Guidance runs at 0.12 strategically against 0.07 tactically, and External Balance abstaining at a 0.19 weight removes the largest potential offset.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The horizons agree, so the view does not need re-establishing across the transition, but its character changes. Tactically it is an event trade into a single dated session on 2026-10-28 where both central banks decide within hours and the market prices only 7-12bp of the 25bp net move we expect. Strategically it is a carry-positive divergence hold through 2026-12-09, where only one of the two banks publishes a track. The estimated vol surface is flat with no event premium at the front, so there is no decay argument for waiting until after the October decision; and a rolled long collects roughly 75bp annualised rather than paying time, which is the specific reason this thesis tolerates being right slowly. Pass-2 execution note: take profit on the tactical tranche in the 0.8080–0.8130 band after 2026-10-28, and hold the strategic tranche with its stop moved up to 0.7960 (the top of the five-touch support) once a daily close above 0.8146 is printed.

catalysts.event: Canada merchandise trade balance for August, plus Ivey PMI; Global Dairy Trade Event 413 the same day
catalysts.rationale: The one session in the window that tests both legs of the terms-of-trade channel at once. The Canadian July balance collapsed to +C$0.77bn from +C$4.2bn with exports to the US down 6.6%, and this is the first print covering a full month of the 50% Section 338 duty regime; a further narrowing is kiwi-positive for the cross. GDT 413 is the opposite test, where a move of more than 3% in the index moves the base leg directly after a +0.9% and -1.1% pair in September.

catalysts.event: Canada Labour Force Survey for September, released alongside US non-farm payrolls
catalysts.rationale: August Canadian employment fell 41,700 against a +15,100 forecast with permanent-employee wage growth halving to 2.0%. A second negative print pushes unemployment above 6.6% and forces hike premium out of the Canadian two-year, which widens the bilateral differential in the kiwi's favour without the RBNZ doing anything. A sharp rebound is the cleanest single way this catalyst goes the other way.

The quote leg's core is already below target at a 1.95% trim-median average while the headline of 3.0% rests on gasoline at +22.8% year on year and decelerating. A headline decaying toward 2.7-2.9% with trim and median unchanged removes the public rationale for Bank of Canada tightening two days before the base leg publishes its own, much hotter, inflation print - the sequencing itself is bilaterally powerful.

The last dairy auction before the New Zealand CPI and the double central-bank decision. Dairy is roughly a quarter of New Zealand goods exports and has no Canadian counterpart, so it is the one commodity that moves the base leg in isolation; a cumulative rise of more than 5% across the two October auctions would materially offset the crude-driven income transfer running the other way.

Consensus is 3.9% year on year against the RBNZ's +0.8% quarterly assumption, with upside risk from a roughly 5% September rise in Brent. An upside print locks in the 28 October hike and, landing two days after a Canadian print expected to decay, widens the measured core inflation gap between the two economies at exactly the moment both central banks are about to decide.

catalysts.event: Reserve Bank of New Zealand OCR decision - Monetary Policy Review
catalysts.rationale: A 25bp hike to 3.00% is about 75% priced and is the modal outcome. The hike itself is largely in the price, so the bilateral content is in the combination: delivered against a Bank of Canada hold on the same day it widens the differential to +75bp, which is more than the roughly 7-12bp of net widening the two curves jointly price. A hold would be the sharpest single negative for the cross in the window. (Pass-2 note: some reports now put the odds at about 80%, and the 2026-09-02 precedent shows that the language matters more than the decision.)

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision with Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.rationale: The higher-leverage half of the double decision and the one with the projection round. The Bank must publish an oil assumption against its governor's stated USD 100 threshold while WTI trades below it, and it debuts a new inflation model in the same session. A hold with a lowered oil assumption is a dovish revision against a two-year carrying 112bp of hike premium, and it lands within hours of the RBNZ hiking. (Pass-2 note: as of 2 October, OIS pricing implied a 74% hold probability with a +7bp market-implied move.)

catalysts.event: FOMC decision (date carried from the quote-currency dossier; the gated meeting file supplied for this pass covers only NZD and CAD)
catalysts.rationale: A shared dollar shock that largely cancels in a cross between two dollar-bloc commodity currencies, which is why the expected impact is Neutral rather than directional. The residual matters only through the funding-vulnerability differential: the base leg has no Fed swap line and a current account deficit to fund, so a hawkish hold that extends the dollar grind leans mildly against the pair.

The first auction of the strategic window and of the peak New Zealand milk season, when offer volumes are largest. Because dairy is the only major commodity with exposure on one leg and none on the other, the auctions are the cleanest bilateral commodity signal available on this cross and they run fortnightly, giving a higher-frequency read than either trade balance.

The September poll projected 64 of 120 seats for the governing bloc against 56, so a clear result is close to neutral. A hung parliament with drawn-out coalition talks into late November would add a modest base-leg risk premium; a Labour-led win would imply looser fiscal policy that the RBNZ would have to lean against, which is mildly supportive through the rates channel and mildly negative through the risk premium.

catalysts.event: Canada Q3 GDP and monthly GDP for September
catalysts.rationale: The first full quarter under the Section 338 duty regime that began 2026-08-22, against a governor's estimate of below 1% for the fourth quarter if tariffs persist. Monthly tracking has already stalled at 0.0% then +0.2% after a 3.3% annualised second quarter. A weak print confirms the growth differential running in the base currency's favour and removes the activity argument for Bank of Canada tightening.

catalysts.event: Reserve Bank of New Zealand OCR decision - Monetary Policy Statement with a new OCR track
catalysts.rationale: The most important scheduled base-leg event of the strategic window and the asymmetry at its heart: the RBNZ publishes a new track, likely lifting the 3.28% peak toward 3.50%, on the same day the Bank of Canada issues a bare statement with no projection round. Only one of the two banks has a scheduled mechanism to raise its own published path before 2027. (Pass-2 note: ANZ expects an October hike, a pause in December, then two further 25bp hikes in February and March, so December is about the track, not a hike.)

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision - fixed announcement date, no Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.rationale: If the Bank has still not moved by this meeting the market's roughly two-hikes-by-January pricing becomes untenable and the 112bp of premium in the Canadian two-year is most likely to be given back here. The absence of a projection round matters bilaterally: the Bank has no vehicle to re-anchor expectations on the same day its counterpart publishes a fresh upward track.

catalysts.event: USTR target date for USMCA interim agreements
catalysts.rationale: The single largest risk to the bullish cross view. An interim deal suspending the Section 338 import bans removes the standing risk premium on the quote leg in one headline and would turn Event Risk from Bullish to Neutral at a stroke; failure entrenches an annually renegotiated treaty through 2036 as a permanent discount on Canadian assets. No published forecast embeds either outcome, so both are unpriced.

assumptions: Price series as delivered: dataPoints 130; dateRange '2026-04-06 to 2026-10-02'; spot 0.80013; spotDate '2026-10-02'; computationRange '2007-12-24 to 2026-10-02 (4900 weekday bars)'; weekendBarsDropped 0. The dataQuality lines are reproduced verbatim: 'NZD/CAD: only 6 resistance / 2 support zones met the 2-touch threshold — supplement with round numbers and note the shortfall'; 'NZD/CAD: 4900 weekday bars in the store (2007-12-24 to 2026-10-02); 1007 weekly, 500 monthly; 130 daily bars passed downstream (2026-04-06 to 2026-10-02), which is the 1-6 month strategic horizon'.

Spot timing: spotDate (2026-10-02) is one session after the 2026-10-01 valuation date, not before it. The valuation-date close was 0.79714. Every level, pip distance, percentage and target in this report is computed against the payload spot of 0.80013. No web-quoted spot is used.
Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day (weekday) closes over the full stored history. Realised vol is annualised on 252 days. ATR(14) is 52 pips.

Zone distances are as computed by the store, measured to the zone midpoint. Edge distances are added where they affect a decision. The 0.7981–0.8059 band, labelled resistance by the store, straddles spot and is treated as a pivot. Because only two support zones qualified, support is supplemented with the round numbers 0.8000, 0.7900, 0.7850 and 0.7800.

Implied vol is the store's triangle estimate: 7.331% at 36.7 days and 7.157% at 99.7 days (atmIv3mPct 7.157 at 99.7 days, not 90). Implied correlation is 0.5626. The store documents that the method runs 9–18% low, so it is quoted as a floor. No risk reversal, IV percentile or barrier data exist because no option is listed on the pair (iv_percentile is therefore null).

Forwards and carry are derived from the futures-implied roll of 75.2bp (actual/365). That figure combines the rate differential and the basis and is not presented as the policy differential, which is +50bp. In the structured carry field a long earns, so annualised_carry_bps is positive (+75.2); prose elsewhere that writes the roll as −75.2bp refers to the forward-discount convention.
Rates block: the 10-year yields are monthly (2026-08-01) and are not quoted as live levels. Live dossier prints are cited separately.

Weights: the four adjustments in the synthesis table apply. They sum to 1.00 on both horizons. In the structured adjustments array the default/applied weights are tactical values; strategic values are stated in each reason.

Verdict handling: all factor stances, confidences, evidence types, weights, contributions, net scores, convictions, rationales, rankings, consensus divergence and cross-horizon text are carried verbatim from pass 1. Pass-2 additions are labelled: the Factor 1 cross-reference, the Factor 9 technicals and implementation, the verdict note and execution notes, and the consensus quantification. None of them changes a score. Where the price data disagrees with the verdict (the downtrend structure and the 2026-09-02 reaction), the disagreement is published openly instead of being worked into the scores.

Pass-1 assumptions carried forward: the CORRA OIS / prediction-market range for BoC pricing; RBNZ pricing from secondary reporting; the corrupt cached Brent series excluded; positioning windows that are short; dossier inputs used despite being past their freshness dates (NZ Q2 CPI, July REINZ, Budget 2026, the Fitch 2025-11-13 note); bilateral trade taken verbatim from IMF DOTS (NZ exports USD 0.7bn and imports USD 0.4bn in 2024; CAD-reported imports from NZ USD 0.9bn and exports to NZ USD 0.3bn; net NZ surplus USD 0.2bn); and FOMC dates sourced from the quote dossier.
Scenario probabilities use the fixed 50/25/25 split. Expected values are computed on unhedged scenario outcomes and, separately, with the stated stops.

No bank-research forecast for NZD/CAD was located, so bank_consensus_forecast is null rather than filled. The only pair-level numbers found are a retail aggregator (exchangerates.org.uk, showing a two-provider consensus of 0.83 for Q4 2026 and 0.85 for Q1 2027, but the page is dated well outside the freshness window and does not name the providers) and extrapolation sites (LongForecast, gov.capital, stockinvest), which are model scripts on ad-supported pages and are a category error as a consensus source. The nearest usable institutional anchors are indirect: six of seven banks surveyed on 2026-09-28 forecast USD/CAD below spot for Q4 2026 at an average of 1.40 (a constructive loonie view), while the Trading Economics model path has NZD/USD at 0.57 at end-Q4 and 0.58 at twelve months (a mildly constructive kiwi view); combined, these imply a consensus for this cross that is roughly flat to slightly lower.

Formatting note: the CAD CFTC percentile (53) is approximated as the CAD leveraged net short of 46,861 relative to the August extreme of 88,897; the NZD percentile (56) is the stated position within the two-month all-spec range. The 52-week range and percentile use the closing basis (0.78606–0.82902, 33rd percentile); the intraday range is 0.78523–0.82962 (34th percentile).
